Attainment and Attendance in Eastbourne

What the national model behind How to Pull the Right Lever says about the district’s secondary schools, within East Sussex and alongside Brighton and Hove. Draft for discussion.

Author
Affiliation

Adam Dennett

Bartlett Centre for Advanced Spatial Analysis, University College London

Published

October 31, 2026

WarningDraft for discussion

One of the district documents for Sussex. It sits beneath the East Sussex document, and the district summary compares all of the districts. Every figure comes from published Department for Education data and the national models of How to Pull the Right Lever. Nothing uses pupil-level records. The commentary is written to a common pattern from the figures; read it as a starting point for discussion.

Summary

Eastbourne’s results are among the weakest of England’s districts, on an intake more disadvantaged than England’s. Its 6 state secondary schools are in Eastbourne.

  • Overall results: 42.7 in Attainment 8 in 2024/25, 226th of 264 districts in England.
  • Disadvantage: 30.0% of pupils are disadvantaged, against 28.3% nationally.
  • Disadvantaged pupils average 33.2, below the national 37.8 (218th of 264).
  • The gap between disadvantaged pupils and the rest is 13.9 points, the 91st widest of 264.

The other findings:

  • For all pupils, Eastbourne is 3.4 points below England. The largest pieces in the national model are prior attainment (-2.3) and Ofsted ratings (-0.5). The district’s schools take 0.2 points beyond what the model expects.
  • For disadvantaged pupils it is 3.5 points below England. The largest pieces are prior attainment (-1.6) and being in the South East (-1.3), and the schools take 0.2 points beyond what the model expects.
  • A district effect on the published model disappears once each school’s own record is counted. On the published model Eastbourne differs from the rest of East Sussex for absence (-8.2%), but that difference belongs to particular schools, not to the place.
  • 2 of the 6 schools are above expectation over 2021/22 to 2024/25. The strongest is St Catherine’s College (+1.3); the weakest Gildredge House (-2.1).
  • Absence was 8.8% in autumn and spring 2025/26 (8.7% a year earlier), against 8.0% for England and 8.9% for East Sussex. Over 2021/22 to 2024/25 its schools ran 0.4 points below what their intakes predict, and The Turing School more than a point above.
  • Reduced timetables run at 1.5 times the national rate, and suspensions at 1.2 times (24.9 per 100 pupils, against 21.2).
  • Disadvantaged groups are small, 33 to 67 pupils a year per school. Every school-level figure for them moves from year to year and should be read over several years.

1 About this analysis

Eastbourne is a district of East Sussex, not a local authority, and that shapes what can be said:

  • The national models place schools in local authorities. The “local authority effect” in this document is East Sussex’s, shared with every school in the county.
  • What is particular to Eastbourne shows up in its schools’ own residuals, and in the district test of Section 6.
  • Absence and exclusions are summed over the district’s 6 schools, followed through any change of URN.

The methods are described in full in the East Sussex document.

For all pupils, Eastbourne is 3.4 points below England. The pieces of at least a quarter of a point:

  • prior attainment (-2.32);
  • Ofsted ratings (-0.55);
  • being in the South East (-0.46);
  • East Sussex’s county-wide effect (+0.46);
  • the level of disadvantage (-0.32);
  • and the district’s schools themselves (-0.22), beyond what the model expects.

For disadvantaged pupils, Eastbourne is 3.5 points below England. The pieces of at least a quarter of a point:

  • prior attainment (-1.57);
  • being in the South East (-1.32);
  • Ofsted ratings (-0.50);
  • admissions (-0.30);
  • East Sussex’s county-wide effect (+0.29);
  • and the district’s schools themselves (-0.20), beyond what the model expects.

5 The disadvantaged gap, school by school

1 of the 6 schools is above expectation for non-disadvantaged pupils and more than a point below it for disadvantaged ones: The Turing School. The Eastbourne Academy is above expectation for both groups. The table below gives each school’s own persistent effect, from the model with a school term, which is the steadier measure.

6 Is there an Eastbourne effect?

The district test of the East Sussex document adds a district level to the national model, with and without each school’s own record.

On the published model, Eastbourne differs from the rest of East Sussex for absence (-8.2%). With each school’s own record in the model, none of that remains: the difference belongs to particular schools, not to the district as a place.

7 Absence

  • 8.8% absence in autumn and spring 2025/26, against 8.0% for England and 8.9% for East Sussex. A year earlier it was 8.7%.
  • Persistent absence is 23.1%, against 21.6% for England.
  • Against its intake, the district’s schools run 0.40 points below what their pupils’ profiles predict, on average over 2021/22 to 2024/25.
  • The Turing School runs more than a point above its predicted absence.
  • The Cavendish School, Gildredge House and Ratton School run more than a point below their predictions.

Reduced timetables account for 0.45% of sessions, against 0.29% in England, 1.5 times the national rate. The Eastbourne Academy’s rate is the highest in the district.

4 of the 6 schools are above the national average absence in 2024/25. Bringing them to it would add up to 4.3 points for all pupils, as an indication of scale.

Suspensions were 24.9 per 100 pupils in 2024/25, against 21.2 for England and 28.0 for East Sussex.

9 Questions for discussion

  1. Disadvantaged pupils. They average 33.2 in Eastbourne against 37.8 in England, and the district’s schools take 0.2 points for them beyond what the model expects. What do St Catherine’s College and The Eastbourne Academy, above expectation for these pupils, do that the district’s other schools could share?
  2. Attendance is not the district’s main lever. Absence makes almost no difference to its results against England, though The Turing School runs more absence than its intake predicts.
  3. Schools, not the place. The district’s apparent effect belongs to particular schools; the question is what is happening in them.
  4. Practice. In Eastbourne, reduced timetables run at 1.5 times the national rate. These are choices made within schools, and neighbouring districts make them differently.
  5. The county. East Sussex’s own effect for disadvantaged pupils is +0.9% (60th of 151), not distinguishable from zero. The county questions in the East Sussex document apply here as well.

Notes on method

Methods and sources are those of the East Sussex document. District membership comes from each school’s postcode (ONS postcode directory, via postcodes.io). Absence and exclusions for the district are summed over its schools, including any predecessor or successor URNs. This document is generated from templates/district_report.qmd by R/20_district_reports.R, from data built by R/17_area_analysis.R, R/18_district_effects.R and R/19_trust_effects.R. Its format is described in AREA_REPORTS.md.
